stem:
During active labour at 40 weeks, a registrar reviews the CTG. The baseline is 145 beats/min with variability of 10 beats/min. With most contractions the fetal heart rate falls within 10 seconds to about 105 beats/min, stays there for 20 seconds and returns to baseline within 10 seconds. Each fall starts at about the same time as the contraction begins.

How should these decelerations be described?

options.label: A
options.text: Early decelerations, as each one begins with its contraction
options.explanation: Early decelerations fall slowly and mirror the contraction; these fall and recover within seconds, which defines variable decelerations even when they are timed with contractions.

options.label: B
options.text: Late decelerations, as they recur with most contractions
options.explanation: Late decelerations fall gradually and reach their lowest point well after the contraction peak, whereas these are abrupt.

options.label: C
options.text: Prolonged decelerations, as they repeat with contractions
options.explanation: A prolonged deceleration lasts more than 90 seconds; these last about 40 seconds from onset to recovery.

options.label: D
options.text: A sinusoidal pattern with regular dips in the heart rate
options.explanation: A sinusoidal pattern is a smooth, regular undulating baseline with absent variability; this trace has normal variability and discrete dips.

options.label: E
options.text: Variable decelerations, from their rapid fall and recovery
options.explanation: A rapid fall and recovery defines a variable deceleration, whatever its timing; early decelerations fall slowly and mirror the contraction, so a quick fall that begins with the contraction is still variable.

context: Classify decelerations by their shape first: an abrupt fall and recovery is variable, even when each one coincides with a contraction.
